According to recent reports, unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

Sources indicate that while orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Sources indicate that cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

In a recent development, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christmas might get the lights, presents, and monthlong buildup, but Ina Garten has a few thoughts about which holiday really deserves the fuss. And if a certain Thanksgiving side dish comes up in conversation, the Barefoot Contessa’s face might tell you everything you need to know.

Recent findings suggest that during the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, the cookbook author asked guest Rose Byrne about her first Thanksgiving in the United States. The Australian actress recalled attending a Friendsgiving, with everyone contributing something to the meal, and Garten immediately wanted to know whether the whole thing had been organized in advance or “if everyone just showed up with string beans.”.

Things got even funnier when Byrne mentioned candied yams topped with marshmallows, something she found “pretty weird.” Garten visibly grimaced at the mention of the dish, chuckling before describing them as “very American." Judging by that expression alone, I wouldn't expect to find the dish making an appearance at her next dinner party.

Garten's feelings about Thanksgiving itself, however, are considerably warmer, especially when compared to Christmas.

In a recent development, "Thanksgiving is just quiet. It's all that one day and it's all about the food," she explained, pointing out that Christmas comes with gifts, parties, and a whole lot more going on.

It makes sense coming from someone who’s built an entire career around bringing people together over a good meal. And we already know Garten’s enthusiasm for Thanksgiving extends beyond what’s on the plate. Last year, she shared her favorite wines to serve with Thanksgiving dinner, including Morgon, a lighter French red from the Beaujolais region, and white Burgundies like Meursault or Montrachet to accompany the turkey. She also likes a Sonoma Valley Pinot Noir, giving the American holiday a little hometown representation in the wine department.

How to Pack for Vegas Like a Vogue Editor

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after years of over-packing, under-packing, and everything in between, I’d like to think I’ve finally mastered the art of packing for a work trip. Most of my work trips take me to the fashion capitals, where I can more or less anticipate what my itinerary–and, naturally, my personal lookbook–will entail. After countless fashion months, I have a fairly reliable formula down–but every now and then, a destination comes along that throws my blueprint for a loop. My latest challenge? Las Vegas for the F1 Grand Prix.

It has been revealed that why is packing for Vegas so difficult? Mainly because dressing for the glitz of Sin City falls rather outside my usual minimalist style. But, as a devoted F1 fan, I decided to embrace the challenge.

I was headed out there to celebrate the launch of the fresh, limited edition Wynn Las Vegas x Olivia Von Halle collection, so I knew there were a few event-specific outfits I needed to prepare. My action-packed itinerary (and hyper-glam Las Vegas alter ego) required sparkles, velvet, and more than a few statement jackets, so I started there, but generally my packing philosophy for all work trips is fairly simple. I start with understanding my itinerary, then work in outfits. I like to scribble my packing list by hand, try on the full look before it makes it to my suitcase (unless I have worn it before), and sometimes commit to a mirror selfie as a reminder. Once I have the key looks figured out, I typically throw a few wardrobe staples in as back-ups. A great pair of denim, black pointed-toe heels, a few white t-shirts, and a black clutch always come with me.

In a recent development, my first stop on this trip was brunch at the recently opened Zero Bond, hosted by Olivia Von Halle and Kelly Piquet. They brought together a mix of familiar faces from the worlds of fashion and Formula 1, including Susie Wolff, CEO of F1 Academy, Bianca Bustamante, racing driver, and jewelry designer Isabela Gruttman. Beyond the collection launch, there was no shortage of entertainment. From being able to look out my window and see the race track, to race cars installed between blackjack tables, to a host of driver pop-up activations, Formula 1 truly took over the city and the energy was incredible.

Ahead, everything I packed and wore for a long weekend work trip to Las Vegas.

It has been revealed that simple, comfortable, and practical is always my philosophy when it comes to a travel outfit. My Away luggage comes with me on every trip, and my travel uniform remains the same as always: a white t-shirt, Agolde denim, Nike sneakers, and in this case, my largest coat that simply could not fit in my suitcase.

I picked up this custom pearl-embroidered Róhe jacket during Paris Fashion Week this past season. It’s heavy and added several pounds to my suitcase, but felt brunch-appropriate styled with a simple black slip skirt and Chanel pumps.

Sources indicate that this festive velvet red jacket from Liberowe was certainly on-theme. By day, I wore the jacket with a simple white tee, jeans, and a faux fur snood; then, for an evening at the casino, I switched it up with the matching mini skirt, sheer tights, and patent heels.

Race night was just incredible; but the dressing brief was tough. I needed a statement-making outfit that was appropriate for the Wynn Skybox but warm enough to spend a few hours outdoors. With 352 overtakes and 31 lead changes, it was nearly impossible to take my eyes off the track… thankfully, I stayed cozy in the Maeve shearling jacket from Ducie. Then came a swift change for my after-party look, where I traded denim for sequins with this semi-sheer Alfie dress, and styled it out with the same giant shearling and a Julietta collar necklace.

There are a few things I never leave behind when traveling for work; good skincare, luxurious pajamas, and jewelry are at the top of that list. I’m quite particular about keeping to my usual morning and evening routines, even when I’m away. My travel skincare is an extension of what I use at home, with a few indulgences that make the end of a long day feel slightly more familiar. The same goes for sleepwear; I almost exclusively travel with a pajama set from Olivia von Halle, this time in an on-theme casino print!

Great jewelry is truly what makes every look your own, and thanks to Michael Rider at Celine my collection has been growing recently… including a dice charm I purchased on this trip as a very chic souvenir.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks.
  • It has been revealed that most recipes serve multiple people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

Recent findings suggest that the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s key that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

It has been revealed that most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

Recent findings suggest that while potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

In a recent development, mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Sources indicate that slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

Industry News: The 7 Most Common Mistakes Home Cooks Make When Cooking Mashed Potatoes

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting.
  • Mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical.
  • Sources indicate that thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting. They're the perfect vessel for a puddle of gravy, and they’re a creamy complement to everything else on your plate—yes, even your aunt's questionable green bean casserole.

Mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical. And yet, we've all somehow still eaten bad ones. With a recipe this basic, even the smallest mistakes have nowhere to hide.

Sources indicate that thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable. We rounded up the most common ways to mess up mashed potatoes so that yours turn out as delicious as possible this holiday season.

It doesn’t matter if you cut your potatoes into a fine dice or rough chunks. Whatever size you pick, stick with it. Making sure your potato pieces are roughly the same size will help them all cook at the same rate. If your knife work is haphazard, you may end up with some pieces that are perfectly cooked, others that are waterlogged and mushy, and some that are still firm in the center.

Like pasta, potatoes need a good amount of seasoning to really shine—which is why salting the cooking water is so crucial. You can be generous with the salt, since much of it stays in the water and ends up going down the drain. When you start seasoning early in the cooking process, it’s easier to build flavor and adjust as you go.

In the hustle of cooking all of your Thanksgiving dishes, you may be tempted to boil your potatoes ahead of time and mash them later in the day. But it’s always better to work with potatoes while they’re still hot and easier to mash. Waiting until they’re cool will likely require far more elbow grease—and you’ll still end up with uneven chunks.

It has been revealed that A smooth, creamy mash is the height of decadence. To make sure the potatoes are lump-free, some people may reach for a blender—but this is one of the most consequential mistakes you can make. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and the more you work them, the more starch gets released from their cell walls. Breaking out the blender may be well-intentioned, but it can leave you with potatoes that are gummy and gluey. Instead, opt for the right tool, like a hand masher, food mill, or potato ricer.

Recent findings suggest that another important thing to consider is that potato starches continue absorbing moisture as mashed potatoes sit. They can soak up the milk you’ve added, leaving your potatoes dry and dense. Don’t be afraid to add more liquid—or at least keep some extra on hand to loosen up your mash before serving.

Anthony Bourdain famously pointed to generous amounts of salt and butter as part of what makes restaurant food taste so good. That’s especially true for mashed potatoes. You may be scared to add more than a light sprinkle of salt, but don’t forget to taste and adjust the seasoning before serving. A little extra salt can make all the difference for your Thanksgiving dinner.

Whether you’re feeding your immediate family or a small army, you should always make a massive batch of mashed potatoes. This side is one of the most popular components of a Thanksgiving menu, so it never hurts to make extra. It’s also one of the most versatile dishes for repurposing leftovers. You can transform them into gnocchi, shepherd’s pie, or crispy fried croquettes. It may require more mashing in the moment, but your future self will thank you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our upcoming app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor.

Recent findings suggest that armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor.

Recent findings suggest that with a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Sources indicate that there is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

It has been revealed that one of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

In a recent development, my Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

It has been revealed that since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor.

It has been revealed that there’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s getting increasingly difficult to keep up with all the limited-edition tumblers, advent calendars, and seasonal releases that disappear off shelves before you’ve finished your morning coffee. And now IHOP is giving breakfast lovers another reason to make room in their kitchen cabinets.

It has been revealed that delish can exclusively reveal that IHOP is launching its first-ever Collector's Holiday Mug on Monday, November 30, with the mugs being sold at participating restaurants nationwide. It’s also the very first time the pancake chain has ventured into selling merchandise directly to customers—and, as it turns out, the idea has been brewing for quite some time.

Recent findings suggest that according to Samantha Strong, IHOP’s executive director of brand calendar strategy, the company has heard from enough coffee-loving customers over the years to realize there was an actual appetite for owning an IHOP mug. “What started as a frequent question has grown into a genuine fan obsession,” she remarked, and this holiday release is now the company's first attempt to turn that enthusiasm into something people can actually buy.

Recent findings suggest that IHOP indicates coffee is its second best-selling menu item, which means an awful lot of people have spent their mornings clutching one of those mugs while waiting for breakfast. But before you start planning an entire IHOP-themed kitchen makeover, know that each participating location will have just 24 (yes, only 24!) mugs available. Once they're gone, they’re gone, at least as far as this limited-time release is concerned.

There's certainly no shortage of things to collect this holiday season, but at least this one’s something you can actually put to use while doing some damage to a stack of pancakes.

#100384. For Malin Åkerman, ‘The Hunting Wives’ Is (Still) a Dream Come True

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2862 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

For Malin Åkerman, ‘The Hunting Wives’ Is (Still) a Dream Come True

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that “Girl, that one’s always a good one,” Malin Åkerman claims.
  • “She was just a young, stupid girl who fell in love, and it was really wrong.
  • In a recent development, some of that sympathy also exists in the way Åkerman plays the audacious, gun-toting, bisexual Texas queen Margo Banks in Netflix’s The Hunting Wives, based on May Cobb’s novel, which returns for season two this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “Girl, that one’s always a good one,” Malin Åkerman claims. I’ve just told her how many times I’ve rewatched her 2008 rom-com 27 Dresses, in which she played the charming, wedding dress-and-crush-stealing Tess, younger sister to Katherine Heigl’s responsible Jane. Tess is, in my view, one of the great 2000s-era villains—though Åkerman doesn’t see her as such.

“She was just a young, stupid girl who fell in love, and it was really wrong. That’s your sister’s crush. Don’t do that, girl. Not cool.” She laughs. “But there was a life lesson in it, and she learned and she grew from it. It’s less villain, more just human.”.

In a recent development, some of that sympathy also exists in the way Åkerman plays the audacious, gun-toting, bisexual Texas queen Margo Banks in Netflix’s The Hunting Wives, based on May Cobb’s novel, which returns for season two this week. Margo has done some bad things, but she’s certainly looked good doing ’em—and former Democratic campaign strategist Sophie (Brittany Snow) can’t help but be drawn into her orbit. Their Bonnie-and-Clyde love story continues in the new season, and the stakes have never been higher.

Here, Åkerman talks to Vogue about the Margos in her own life, performing with Snow at the Las Culturistas Culture Awards, and why it’s the perfect time to watch a show about lesbians in Texas.

Vogue: It’s a great time to be releasing a show about Texas.

It has been revealed that malin Åkerman: It’s unbelievable. There was a great little picture, Dermot [Mulroney] sent it to us gals, and it was like, “The Hunting Wives Turns Texas Votes,” or something like that. All the lesbians came out [to vote]. I’m going to misquote it, but it’s out there.

Do you think there’s a future where Jed loses the governor race to–.

It has been revealed that …I was going to say, to Margo Banks? Maybe she takes over, the Lady Macbeth in the back just pulling all the strings.

That could be really fun if he has someone that he’s up against, a powerful female that maybe Margo has an affair with. Let’s see.

Season two demonstrates us a different side of Margo—she’s in a more vulnerable state. I’m curious what you thought of her season two arc. Where do you think her mindset is at the beginning of the show?

Sources indicate that it’s really nice to see the power dynamic shift. Sophie came into her power and Margo’s softening and actually letting someone in, which is huge for a person like Margo, who has been a survivor and keeps everyone at an arm’s length. You see these cracks in her veneer that she’s created for her whole life, really. We start off in a pretty bad place for Margo in season two. She’s in the doghouse, so to speak. She does not like being there.

Sources indicate that I loved playing with her vulnerability and really just softening, enveloped in Sophie’s love and protection. That was really nice because I just don’t think that Margo has ever really had that other than [from] her brother, in a weird way, who was the only person that she trusted. I feel like we finally get to see her trusting someone else. Because she doesn’t really trust Jed, that’s just a means to an end. She knows how to play him, she knows how to do her thing to get what she needs.

The Margo–Jed relationship is interesting this season. He acts like a man with power but he is also very vulnerable to her charms. What kind of discussions were you and Dermot having?

Sources indicate that all men in power are vulnerable to women if they know how to play their cards right. You know what I mean? There are those women out there who know exactly how to get the guys, they know exactly the buttons to push. Dermot and I, we have a lot of fun conversations. We never like it when we have to play angry at each other because we really love each other. All of us, by the way, on this show, we hate when we have to hate each other. But Dermot and I definitely have much more fun when we get to be in love, so to speak. I don’t think Margo actually loves Jed, but it was fun to have those moments.

I just love playing Margo and all her agendas behind everything and trying to play it as real as possible, especially with Jed, because she’s really a player. She’s got Sophie on the side [while she’s] telling Jed that he’s everything. Yeah, Dermot and I have a lot of fun. Mostly we just goof around on set, to be really honest with you.

Well, you guys do have a rom-com that’s coming out in a few weeks.

Listen, Dermot asked me when we were on set—it was the last couple weeks of shooting [season one], it was his last day of shooting. He’s like, “I’m about to go do this rom-com on a cruise.” And I was like, “Nope, not doing it, never. I don’t ever want to go on a cruise, it’s not my thing. Too claustrophobic. Don’t want to be on for three weeks. Are you nuts?” And he goes, “Well, the first week it would just be us and you can bring your family and it’ll become this free vacation.” I was like, “Oh, okay. When do we start?” And he goes, “Four days after you wrap this show.” It’s like, Oh my God. But it was my son’s summer break, so I ended up convincing a girlfriend of mine, one of my best girlfriends who’s also a makeup artist, to come along with her kids on the trip. I don’t know how it’s going to turn out, but we had a blast making it.

It has been revealed that we had a little too much fun. We were like, “Is there even a movie in this? I don’t know, but we’re having a great time.”.

According to recent reports, I’m a significant Dale Dickey fan, and she plays a fun role in this season. What was it like filming with her?

She’s phenomenal on every level. She’s a phenomenal human being—the nicest, loveliest human you’ll ever meet and a phenomenal actress. I remember seeing her in Winter’s Bone and just going, “Wow, this woman is just great.” And what a face—the realism in the expressions. And she’s just beautiful to watch when she works and she really is invested. She believes in her craft and she’s so collaborative and lovely. All the greatest things you can say about a person, I would say about Dale Dickey.

Dale Dickey as Zelda and Cam Gigandet as Gentle John in Episode 204 of The Hunting Wives.

In a recent development, thinking about Margo and Sophie this season, they’re both killers, so they can be on a more even playing field. But Sophie does have this secret at the beginning of the season….

The audience question is, do they really love each other? And listen, that’s an open-ended question. There’s no real answer to that. I think there is love there, for sure. I think on Sophie’s part towards Margo, it’s almost an extension of her addictive personality. Margo’s an addiction. Margo fluctuates between necessity and love because Margo’s just not honest with herself. She’s not open, honest, and vulnerable, so you can’t be that with someone else.

I felt like there were parts of this season where Sophie was scarier than Margo.

In a recent development, totally. You let the beast out and you’re like, Holy shit, she needs something. She’s going to get it. That’s also what attracts these two to each other, is that drive. You get to see why they’re kind of meant for each other in this season. It’s not just Margo. Margo’s not just the crazy one and the wild one. Sophie’s got it in her, she just needs to be unleashed.

Have you had a Margo type in your life, or have you been that type? Someone who draws you into their orbit or brings out something in you that you’re like, Oh, I love being around this person?

Yeah, sure. I mean, I think it’s gone both ways. I think I’ve been in the shoes of a Margo and I’ve been attracted to it. I had a little bit of a fun time in between marriages, so to speak, and there were definitely people who were absolutely wrong for me, but I was very drawn in. Also knowing they were wrong for me, but just couldn’t get enough…it’s such a wild experience. And then I also played the part of drawing people in and just using them for what I needed. I knew it wasn’t going to become a relationship, and just having fun with it almost felt…I don’t know, it was a great time. I understand why Margo is having a great time, but [I haven’t experienced] anywhere near the extent of the deception and the games that she plays. But the draw, I can understand that, where there’s just this sexual energy that pulls you in.

Brittany Snow and Akerman in Episode 205 of The Hunting Wives.

According to recent reports, after season one, there was some time where you weren’t totally sure if Hunting Wives was getting picked up again. Now you have a season three renewal already locked in. How does it feel to have that kind of stability?

Sources indicate that it’s a fucking dream come true, it really is. I feel so, so lucky. I love this character, it’s a character of a lifetime. I love the people I get to work with. I couldn’t have wished for it…and it’s a steady job. If this goes for 10 years, I’ll be elated. Although maybe we can make Margo just chill a little bit on the working out and looking top-notch all the time, and tanned and everything. Maybe she just lets herself go a little. Let me just enjoy my pizza and my pasta on a daily basis, okay guys? Let’s not judge.

Do you know when you’ll go back for season three?

According to recent reports, I’m flying out to Atlanta on November 29. We get started December 2. We’re premiering [season two] and then off we go, Season 3. I’m excited. I miss my Hunting Wives family.

According to recent reports, I loved your and Brittany’s performance at the Las Culturistas Culture Awards. How did that come about?

Well, Bowen Yang was sat in front of us at the Emmys, where we ended up surprisingly presenting. We weren’t supposed to present, and so he was with us on that journey. It was so much fun. We were like, “Bowen, we have to present.” He’s like, “What? Right now?” He’s such a lovely person. From that, maybe that seed was planted in his head. We met Matt Rogers as well, and they’re such a great duo. They were the ones who came to us and noted, “We have an idea. Hunting Wives and Heated Rivalry have been such a huge hit in the LGBTQ community that it would be really fun to do this, to have you guys open the whole ceremony.” We were super game for that. Like, “Okay, we’ll wear the hockey jerseys, but we need to bring in the Hunting Wives into it all.”.

Do you think there is any kind of connective tissue that links The Hunting Wives and Heated Rivalry’s success beyond the queer relationships? Do you think there’s anything that both reveals have in common?

Recent findings suggest that I think it’s the forbiddenness of it all. That’s always something that we’re all drawn to because I think we all have our own secret thoughts that we don’t share with everybody. We all have our own fantasies, we all have our own things that we lust [over]. These indicates kind of open them up. Heated Rivalry has a more crucial message in a way, because this is really something that the author was talking about. Being in such a macho world as hockey is, that’s a really brave thing, to come out publicly and to have a relationship publicly within that. I loved it, I thought it was really beautiful.

It’s different from Hunting Wives because Hunting Wives is…we’re a little more on the camp side. We’re true just raw entertainment and craziness, but we have that element of exploring sexuality in a town, in a world, where it’s frowned upon.

I’m sure that Margo and Sophie will be some people’s queer awakening in the years to come.

I sure hope so. Bring it on. Come on out, everybody. It’s a great place to be.

Recent findings suggest that when you think back to when you were in maybe your early or mid-20s, were you dreaming of projects like this? What kind of arc did you want your career to have when you were very young?

It has been revealed that oh, gosh. Early 20s, I didn’t know what I wanted more than five minutes ahead of me. I was not one of those people who was planning ahead and goal-oriented. I was along for the ride. I really was letting life take me. I got swept away in this romantic-comedy film era with 27 Dresses and Heartbreak Kid and Couples Retreat. I was just enjoying every moment of it, not thinking about, Oh, this can come to an end.

It has been revealed that after a few of those romantic comedies, I really started craving something that I could sink my teeth into a little more and to try my hand at drama. I started seeking out little independent films, which is something that I love watching: the little indies or foreign films. That’s when I remember The Ticket came along with Dan Stevens, and Billions came along—I feel like that’s a precursor to Margo Banks, Lara Axelrod.

Recent findings suggest that hunting Wives came at the perfect time because I had had that moment during COVID and after, where there were a lot of projects that were, I call them “yes projects.” I was saying yes because I needed to work, but I wasn’t feeling passionate about them anymore and it was really making me sad. I felt like projects that I really wanted to do, I couldn’t get in the room, and I started to have a lot of, I call them “head gremlins” talking to me, dark voices in my head. The voices telling me, Yeah, this is it. You’re expired. I mean, you had a good run. Say thank you, feel grateful. I just went, No.

For the past five years I’ve been working on my true passion project. Won’t say anything yet, but hopefully it’ll come to fruition. It’s something that I’ve built from the ground up and it’s written, I’ve got a director attached. We just need to get out there and get it made. But other than that, when Hunting Wives came along, it just felt like, oh, this was the hit that I really needed as far as getting passionate again about the work that I’m doing, because I just love this character and this job. It was incredible to not only be passionate about a character, but to feel relevant in my business again.

Do you think your definition of success has changed over the years?

I do think so. Becoming a parent changed all of that. Success for me, really, the most vital success is the success of my family. And in business, I feel like I look back and I go, I’ve had a great career and how lucky am I if it continues? This is wonderful. So I’m happy for this show to have its success because all the people who are in it are so deserving. But success is a really…for me, it’s not linked to my work anymore. It really is linked to, am I successful as a person? Am I succeeding in my day-to-day life? Am I handling life well? In your 20s we talk a lot about being successful and a lot of it is linked to work. And then as we grow older and we realize what’s really important, then it shifts.

I’ve been asking myself those questions a lot lately, like, how do you define yourself outside of work?

Industry observers note that exactly. And that success is, how do people see you and how are you presenting to the world? Have you succeeded in becoming the person that you want to be, the best version of you? And where’s the work still need to be done? I have a 13-year-old boy who still wants to cuddle me at night and tells me he loves me [when I] drop him off at school. He is like, “Bye, Mom. Love you. See you later.” Thirteen. I’m like, “I have succeeded. This is a huge success.”.

More sheet-pan dinners this way.

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling).

In a recent development, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Industry observers note that place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Recent findings suggest that beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Recent findings suggest that reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

In a recent development, place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Sources indicate that pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for new member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.

Sources indicate that trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s latest member orientation. Giddy, even.

The incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

It has been revealed that “I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” mentioned Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

Forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

“I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he noted of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”.

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

Sources indicate that “It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” remarked Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

According to recent reports, cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

“The congressman mentioned that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s notable that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke stated. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”.

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

It has been revealed that “I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” remarked Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

It has been revealed that but just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” noted Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

Industry observers note that “I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he said.

After arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander said he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he stated.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”.

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he remarked.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their fresh workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” said Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

It has been revealed that “They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander remarked.

Interiors, and interiority, are recurring subjects of Charlotte Eskildsen’s collections for The Garment. For pre-fall, the designer imagined a woman living in a townhouse in central Copenhagen near the Marble Church, a very chic area, who wears clothes in “her own really private way... Nothing in this collection is too tied up,” the designer said. “Even if it’s suiting, it will stretch, and it’s comfortable to wear.”.

Some of the garments have a feeling of intimacy that comes from their origin in the boudoir. Lingerie dressing is a trend that Eskildsen isn’t ready to give up as she sees it as an expression of femininity that counters the outward strength often expected of women. So next to a lace-trimmed skirt with an asymmetrically inserted godet and a collarless jacket, the many slip dresses in the collection looked somewhat saccharine and less street-ready than the more structured looks. She’s “dressed, but she doesn’t know if she wants to go out or not,” the designer said of her muse. (This cozy, hazy should-I-or-shouldn’t-I feeling assumes win-win options.).

Recent findings suggest that in betweenness is at the heart of all pre-fall collections which need to adapt to snow and sun. For cooler temps there is a smart cropped black leather jacket shown with tailored white pants. An injection of romance comes in the form of a flowy Daisy Buchanan-ish dress the color of a snowflake with bias cut lines which combines silk chiffon, jacquard, and silk wool. There are “a lot of cut lines to be able to mix all the fabrics so it’s like a blanket of different fabrics,” as Eskildsen put it. Hygge, in other words, but make it haute.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

It has been revealed that the batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

Sources indicate that the secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

No. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

What kind of miso is best for baking?

White and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Is butter mochi cake gluten-free?

According to recent reports, mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

In a recent development, toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too quickly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Sources indicate that A decade ago, many of us wouldn’t leave the house without a full-coverage beat. As Instagram selfies and YouTube tutorials took over pop culture, meticulously sculpted, perfected complexions reigned supreme—until the pendulum swung in the opposite direction, ushering in an era of barely-there coverage and skin-care-infused formulas. And while the early 2020s were defined by ultra-dewy, almost damp-looking skin, today’s complexion ideal strikes a more nuanced balance: coverage without the weight, radiance without the shine.

Sources indicate that “Modern complexion formulations have come such a long way, and the upcoming-Gen complexion products give medium to buildable coverage that glides and melts into skin, while giving a soft-focus matte finish that reads radiant rather than shiny,” says celebrity makeup artist and Vogue Beauty Board member Fara Homidi. “We can now get more coverage, while the final look is breathable and has flex to it, never heavy and cakey.” Nowadays, lightweight texture, skin-friendly ingredients, and flexible coverage are non-negotiable. The ideal product perfects your complexion without looking or feeling like makeup.

“I want the complexion product to be able to be great, without the help of a concealer or bronzer,” notes content creator and fellow Board member Toni Bravo. “It also needs the right undertones that bring out dimension naturally,” she says, to create a second-skin effect.

Mastering your complexion, however, is both the science of formulation and the art of application. While formulas are more advanced than ever, technique and placement have simultaneously evolved. Homidi points out that it’s not about wearing less makeup, but about how it’s placed on the skin. Her best advice is to put the product only where you need it like under the eyes or around the nose, with lighter coverage around the the rest of the face. She prefers pinpointing blemishes and discolorations with fuller coverage, while letting the rest of the skin breathe.

In a recent development, looking ahead, beauty lovers and experts alike can expect complexion makeup to keep evolving. “Hopefully, complexion products continue to evolve shade-wise,” indicates Bravo. “We’ve seen brands truly expand the meaning of inclusivity in the last few years, in ways 14-year-old me wouldn’t believe. Folks understanding undertones, and how to apply them to our complexion products, will make for a more conscious consumer and intentional brand.” Meanwhile, Homidi expects further advancements in texture and innovative application methods (roller ball foundation applicator, anyone?). In short, the future looks more inclusive, with advanced formulations and better shade matches for everyone.

According to recent reports, alongside her many talents, one quality I particularly applaud my mom for is her expertise in hosting. She is specifically known for what she dubbed “the emergency dinner party.” This is the kind of soirée that, despite being rapidly organized—perhaps after a long day at work or a busy weekend afternoon—never fails to keep guests entertained and impressed. When it comes to appetizers at an emergency dinner party, the objective is to use limited ingredients, ensure ease of assembly, and deliver bangin’ flavor. For my mom’s famous feta artichoke dip, only three ingredients are absolutely crucial: feta, artichoke hearts, and olive oil. The brine from the canned artichoke hearts allows the feta to melt down in the oven, which in turn coats the artichoke hearts, creating a velvety dip. My favorite variation includes adding honey, thyme, and an olive topper, which elevates the dip to a whole newly introduced level. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

It has been revealed that house Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” mentioned Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

According to recent reports, republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the newly introduced lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

Newly introduced maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, said he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

According to recent reports, advocates for a latest map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley remarked he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Recent findings suggest that democrats could also look to redraw the lines in Newly introduced York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Fresh York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for upcoming maps in 2028.

According to recent reports, officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

It’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass fresh maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where newly introduced maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, said last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

According to recent reports, democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their new majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he mentioned Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to new maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he remarked.

At Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”.

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the manufacturer imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

According to recent reports, origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its substantial flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

Semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, prepares to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the swiftly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

According to recent reports, remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

I Tested Peloton's Fresh, More Affordable Folding Treadmill
